title: Bangladesh starts China-funded container jetties at Mongla port near Bengal border
dek: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman laid the foundation stone for a Tk 4,068 crore project, nearly nine-tenths of it paid for by China Exim Bank and built by a Chinese state firm. India has its own, long-stalled plan to upgrade the same port.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday laid the foundation stone for two container jetties at Mongla port, a Tk 4,068 crore project paid for mostly with a loan from the Export-Import Bank of China and built by a Chinese state-owned contractor. Mongla, Bangladesh's second-largest seaport, sits on the Pasur river beside the Sundarbans, close to the West Bengal border.

China is lending about Tk 3,593 crore, nearly nine-tenths of the cost, and Bangladesh is paying about Tk 475 crore. The project is meant to give Mongla its first dedicated container-handling jetties and to add about 400,000 containers (measured in twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs) a year of capacity. That is more than ten times the number of containers the port handled last year.

## What happened

Rahman flew to Mongla by helicopter from Dhaka on Thursday morning. According to the state news agency BSS, as carried by Views Bangladesh, the helicopter landed at the port's helipad at 9.50 am Bangladesh time (9.20 am IST). He attended two programmes at the port: the signing of an investment memorandum and the foundation-stone ceremony for the jetties. The Daily Star and The Business Standard (TBS) reported that the memorandum was to be signed between Invest Bangladesh, the government's investment promotion agency, and China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC). The Daily Star also reported that a Chinese delegation led by CRCC's chairman, Dai Hegen, was due to meet the prime minister to discuss infrastructure, industrial investment and special economic zones. The text of the memorandum had not been published by Thursday afternoon.

The project, formally called "Expansion and Modernisation of Facilities at Mongla Port", covers:

- two new container jetties, numbered 10 and 11, with a combined quay length of 368 metres
- a container yard, a container delivery yard and a yard for dangerous goods
- 49 pieces of cargo-handling equipment, which the port authority expects to move more than 30 containers an hour

The engineering, procurement and construction contractor is China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), a subsidiary of CRCC, according to The Daily Star and Maritime Gateway. The port authority's chairman, Rear Admiral Arif Ahmed Mustafa, said construction would begin after the ceremony. Maritime Gateway reported that the project is due to be finished by December 2028.

## How China is paying for it

The China-Bangladesh joint communiqué issued on 26 June, at the end of Rahman's visit to Beijing, lists the "Mongla Port Facilities Modernization and Expansion Project" among the projects the two governments agreed to take forward. The loan agreement followed on 10 October. According to Maritime Gateway, it was signed in Dhaka by Alia Meher, a joint secretary in Bangladesh's Economic Relations Division, and Fengjun Tian of China Exim Bank. The loan is for 2.404 billion yuan, about $336 million. Maritime Gateway reported the terms as 2% interest, repayable over 20 years including a five-year grace period.

Bangladesh's top economic planning body approved a revised version costing Tk 4,068.23 crore in February 2025, Maritime Gateway reported. An earlier version had been costed at Tk 4,282.76 crore.

## Background

Mongla is a small port by regional standards. It handled 29,700 TEUs of containers and 1.22 crore tonnes of cargo in the year to June 2026, according to Mongla Port Authority figures published by The Daily Star. Container traffic rose 38% on the year before. The port has five bulk jetties that also handle containers, no container scanner, and a shallow approach channel, the Pasur, which is being dredged under a five-year programme. It lies about 100 km up-river from the sea.

India has its own stake in the port. Under a 2018 agreement on the use of Chattogram and Mongla ports, Indian goods can be shipped through both ports to and from India's north-eastern states. India also agreed to finance a much larger upgrade of Mongla through a line of credit. In December 2022, The Daily Star reported that the "Upgradation of Mongla Port" project was estimated at Tk 6,014 crore, with Tk 4,459 crore of it to come from the Indian credit line. The Mongla Port Authority signed an Indian consultancy firm, Egis India, to manage it. That project was also meant to add 400,000 TEUs of container capacity and was due for completion by July 2024. A Financial Express (Dhaka) report from November 2022 said work had not started eight years after the loan agreement under India's third credit line was signed. The Declaration could not establish the current status of the Indian-funded project, and neither government mentioned it on Thursday.

The jetties are one of several Chinese projects in Bangladesh's south-west and north. On Wednesday, Liu Haixing, head of the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, told a roundtable in Dhaka that work was "advancing steadily" on a Mongla Port industrial park and on a plan to restore the Teesta river, which flows into Bangladesh from north Bengal.

## What it means for India and Bengal

The project puts a Chinese state-owned company in charge of building and equipping a port near the Indian border and the Sundarbans, the mangrove delta that India and Bangladesh share. There is no public sign that China will operate the jetties: the port authority, a Bangladeshi government body, is the owner. But the equipment, the contractor and most of the money are Chinese, and repayments to China Exim Bank will run into the 2040s.

There are three concrete issues for India:

- **Competition and transit.** Mongla, like the Kolkata and Haldia docks, serves shipping at the head of the Bay of Bengal. Modern container jetties would make it more attractive to shipping lines, and Indian transit cargo can use the port under the 2018 agreement.
- **The Indian-funded project.** The new jetties promise roughly the same container capacity as the larger Indian line-of-credit project. If the Chinese-built jetties go ahead first, it is unclear what role remains for the Indian project.
- **Chinese presence close to the border.** Taken with the Teesta plan near the Siliguri Corridor and Chinese interest in Bangladesh's ports, the project extends China's footprint in infrastructure along India's eastern flank.

## What they are saying

Neither Rahman's office nor the port authority had released the text of his remarks by Thursday afternoon. The port authority's chairman told The Daily Star that the expansion would support economic activity in Bangladesh's south and north-west and could make Mongla an alternative trade gateway, but that attracting cargo and shipping lines, better road links and year-round navigability were key to the project paying off.

China has presented its projects in Bangladesh as development cooperation open to all parties. Liu said in Dhaka on Wednesday that China does "not draw ideological lines". India's Ministry of External Affairs has not commented on the Mongla project. At its briefing on 3 November it said India wanted "constructive" ties with Dhaka.

## What happens next

Construction is due to start now and end by December 2028. The terms of the CRCC investment memorandum have yet to be published. The next fixed date in India-Bangladesh relations is 12 December, when the 1996 Ganges water-sharing treaty expires; the two sides have not yet set a date for talks on renewing it.

## Key numbers

- Tk 4,068 crore: total project cost
- Tk 3,593 crore: China Exim Bank loan (2.404 billion yuan)
- Tk 475 crore: Bangladesh government share
- 368 metres: combined quay length of the two jetties
- About 400,000 TEUs a year: planned added container capacity
- 29,700 TEUs: containers Mongla handled in 2025-26
- December 2028: target completion
